en: Padminī Ratnarakṣita [Chapter 15: Characteristics of the Alms Bowl] *Some corrections by PDSz*

[The Blessed One said: “Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature (*svabhāva*). What are the four? They are: the imagined self-nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), the dependent self-nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the perfected self-nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), and the self-nature of the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna-svabhāva*). “What, Mahāmati, is the imagined self-nature? It is the attachment to names, signs, and characteristics (*nāmanimittalakṣaṇa*) regarding objects that do not exist; it is like seeing a snake in a rope in the dark, or seeing water in a mirage. This is called the imagined self-nature. “What, Mahāmati, is the dependent self-nature? It is the manifestation of the mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*) arising from the habit-energy (*vāsanā*) of false discrimination (*vikalpa*); it is the appearance of objects such as form and so forth, which are devoid of external reality. This is called the dependent self-nature. “What, Mahāmati, is the perfected self-nature? It is the state of the dependent self-nature being forever free from the imagined self-nature; it is the non-dual nature of reality (*tathatā*), the realm of the noble ones (*āryagocara*), and the attainment of the fruit through the power of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpajñāna*). This is called the perfected self-nature. “What, Mahāmati, is the self-nature of the Great Vehicle? It is the realization of the non-arising of all dharmas, the entry into the womb of the Tathāgata (*tathāgatagarbha*), the attainment of the ten stages (*bhūmi*), the mastery of the powers (*bala*), the grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*), and the unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*). This is called the self-nature of the Great Vehicle. Then the Blessed One spoke these verses: “The imagined is like a barren woman’s son, The dependent is like a dream or a city of Gandharvas; The perfected is like space, The self-nature of the Great Vehicle is likewise. “By means of the threefold self-nature, And the five dharmas, I teach the Dharma to the world, To lead them beyond suffering. At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, please explain to me the characteristics of the various vehicles (*yāna*) and the distinctions between the Śrāvaka-vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha-vehicle, and the Tathāgata-vehicle. The Blessed One replied: “Mahāmati, there are three characteristics of the Śrāvaka-vehicle: the realization of the non-existence of a self (*ātman*), the understanding of the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and the attainment of the fruit through the cultivation of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*). These are the characteristics of the Śrāvaka-vehicle. “Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Pratyekabuddha-vehicle has these characteristics: the realization of the non-existence of a self, the understanding of dependent origination, and the attainment of the fruit through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the absence of reliance on a teacher. These are the characteristics of the Pratyekabuddha-vehicle. “Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Tathāgata-vehicle has these characteristics: the realization of the non-arising of all dharmas, the entry into the womb of the Tathāgata, the attainment of the ten stages, the mastery of the powers, the grounds of self-confidence, and the unique qualities of a Buddha. These are the characteristics of the Tathāgata-vehicle. “Mahāmati, these are the distinctions between the vehicles. By means of these distinctions, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones teach the Dharma to sentient beings according to their capacities, in order to lead them to the ultimate cessation of suffering. Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, what is the meaning of the term ‘Tathāgata’? The Blessed One replied: “Mahāmati, the term ‘Tathāgata’ signifies one who has come from suchness (*tathatā*) and gone to suchness; one who has realized the non-duality of subject and object; one who has attained the body of the Dharma (*dharmakāya*) which is unborn and undying; and one who has transcended all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*). For this reason, Mahāmati, he is called a Tathāgata. Thus spoke the Blessed One, and with this the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati and the entire assembly were delighted and rejoiced in what the Blessed One had taught. [End of Chapter on the Characteristics of Self-Nature]

In this context, since a lotus vessel is employed in the worship of the *kumārī* and in the *gaṇacakra* and so forth, he indicates the characteristics of the vessel— whether explicitly enjoined or implied by the force of the circumstances— even though they were not previously mentioned. The passage beginning with "Now" (*atha*) and so on should be understood in the same way elsewhere as well.

Regarding the statement, "In this context, for the worship of young maidens (*kumārī*), the *gaṇacakra*, and so forth, one should employ a lotus vessel," this teaches the characteristics of the vessel—whether explicitly requested or requested by implication. The passage beginning with "Then" (*atha*) and so forth [proceeds] to explain that. One should understand other instances in the same way.

Even clay and other materials possess the nature of a lotus vessel because they have been fashioned into the form of a lotus vessel. Regarding the passage beginning with “*brāhmaṇe*”: it is not by way of the human caste (*manuṣyajāti*), but rather precisely by way of the skull-cast (*kapālajāti*). He demonstrates this very point with the passage beginning with “*śveta*. White is the Brāhmaṇa caste; reddish-white is the Kṣatriya; yellowish-brown is the Vaiśya; dark is the Śūdra. The inversion [of the order] is for the sake of metrical requirements. One who has the color of ash and so forth is an outcaste (*antyaja*). [The phrase] “the nature of a lotus vessel” refers to clay and the like.
Baroda reads *pītapitapiṅgalam*?
[The emendation is] *vyatyaya*;
[the reading is] *bhasmādivarṇam*.
Regarding "the outcaste" (*antyaja*): although *tya* and *ja* appear to have been cancelled, they are required [by the Tibetan].

Since even those such as the *jim pa* (clay-workers) and others are fashioned in the form of lotus vessels, they are indeed "lotus vessels. Regarding the phrase "the Brahmin" and so forth: this refers not to the human caste, but rather to the skull-cast (*kapāla-jāti*). Those very ones are shown by the words "white" and so forth; "white" refers to the Brahmin caste. "Red" and "white" refer to the Kṣatriya caste.

Yellow and orange-red are the *rājanya* (royal) caste; green is the *vaiśya* (commoner) caste; the variegated [colors] are due to the requirements of poetic meter; and the colors such as ash-gray are the *śūdra* (low) caste.

"Deficient" (*hīna*) means being distorted by the breaking or splitting of the petals, and likewise "excessive" (*adhika*). "Moist" (*ārdrā*) means glossy. Alternatively, by these three terms, the states of inferior, middling, and superior are indicated. The passage beginning with "of form" (*rūpām*) and so forth is easy to understand.

"Inferior" means thin and of poor shape; "superior" is likewise. "Moist" means oily. Alternatively, by these three phrases, the inferior, the middling, and the superior are shown. The passage beginning with "form" is easy to understand.

"Examination" (*parīkṣām*) means investigation. "To the minister" (*mantriṇe*) refers to the minister. "One should accomplish" (*sādhayet*) means one should take hold of. "Killer of Brahmins" (*brahmaghnam*) means that which causes fear to Brahmins and yogins; likewise for "killer of cows. "Devoid of caste" (*varṇahīnam*) means disgraceful. "Breacher of mantras" (*mantrabhedanam*) means that which destroys the attainment of mantra-siddhi. "Non-destructive" (*aghātī*) means not causing harm. The minister should accomplish it; [it is] the breaching of mantras.

"Thoroughly examined" means determined. "By the mantra-practitioner" means by the *mantrin*. "Should be accomplished" means should be adopted. "Destroyer of Brahmins" means that fear arises for the yogins regarding the Brahmins; likewise, it is the "destroyer of cattle. "Base mantra-practitioner" means one who causes [others] to lose their reputation.
"Mantra is destroyed" means that the siddhi of mantra is destroyed. "Unimpaired" means that there is no deterioration.

"Vrataśrāvī" means one whose nature (*śīla*) it is to proclaim (*śravituṃ*) and continuously produce (*prabandhena utpādayituṃ*) the vow (*vrata*). "Āgneyāsya" means having a face toward the southeast (*āgneyīmukha*). "Caura" means a thief-attractor (*caurākarṣaka*). "Strīghātī" means a destroyer of the wife of the holder (*dhārakasya strīvināśakṛt*). "Caṇḍāla" means a killer of female slaves and so forth (*dāsyādighātikam*). [To produce...]

"Continuous observance" (*vrata-santati*) means that which produces [results] through continuity; it refers to ethical discipline (*śīla*). "Possessing fire" means facing toward the fire. "Robber" means one who summons thieves. "Destroyer of women" means one who ruins the wife of the one who maintains [the vow]. "Fierce" means one who destroys servants and so forth.

"He should be a *pīṭha*" means he should be untiring in wandering through sacred seats (*pīṭha*) and so forth. "*Maṇḍaleśvara*" means one who is highly honored. "*Sādhakasiddhim*" means that which effects the desired accomplishment for the practitioner (*sādhaka*). The sense is that it brings about whatever specific accomplishment (*siddhi*) the practitioner strives to achieve. *Maṇḍaleśvara*.

"Will become a locus" means that one will not be weary of proceeding to the [meditative] loci and so forth. "Lord of the mandala" means that one should perform many offerings. "The accomplishment of the practitioner" means that it accomplishes the desires of the practitioner; the intention is that it brings about the perfection of whatever accomplishment one wishes to achieve.

"Four-part" (*catuṣkala*) means having four sections. "Alms-gathering" (*bhaikṣaka*) means that which produces the acquisition of alms. "Fruitless for the accomplishment of supernatural powers" (*siddhisādhananiṣphalam*) means fruitless for the accomplishment of powers such as pacification (*śānti*); the intention is that it is, however, appropriate for [rites involving] cruelty. He says "some," etc., because the caste must also be determined by the force of the [auditory] stream. And this water should be known after filling [the vessel]. "Fruitless for the accomplishment of pacification, etc. (emended from *nisphalam*).
Even though it is fruitless,
[there is] birth.

"Fourth" refers to the fourth section. "Beggar" means one who obtains alms. "There is no fruit for accomplishing the siddhis" means that there is no fruit for accomplishing siddhis such as pacification (*śānti*) and so forth; the intention is that [such rites] should be applied to wrathful (*raudra*) activities.

It is said that "by means of the [shape of the] opening as well, one should determine the caste and so forth," which refers to the passage beginning with "the opening" (*bu ga*). These should also be understood by pouring water [into them].

"Possessing the luster of a lotus and marked by a lotus" means that it is perfectly round in its configuration, like a blooming lotus, either by way of its shape or its color. "Born from a pearl-oyster shell" (*śuktija*) means that it is white like a string of pearls because of its abundance of white spots.

By virtue of its color, [it is called] "lotus-like" because its shape is perfectly round like a blooming lotus and by virtue of its very color. By virtue of being "with pearls," it possesses a row of white *bindu*s resembling a string of pearls.

This has been said: having examined the skull-bowls (*kapāla*) of those fallen on the battlefield during the time of combat, or of those discarded in great cemeteries (*mahāśmaśāna*), one that is free from the aforementioned defects and endowed with the qualities as described must necessarily be worn by the yogin. This concludes the commentary on the fifteenth chapter. || 0 ||
It must certainly be worn.

As it has been said: having examined the skull of one who has died in battle on a battlefield, or one who has been cast away in a great charnel ground and so forth, and having avoided the faults of its location, a yogin must certainly wear one that possesses the qualities as they have been described. This concludes the commentary on the fifteenth chapter.
